statements.quote: This is also my foray into paid content. So the idea is I’m going to write things, like this piece, which will presumably not be opinion pieces, although I will, likely, express opinions.
statements.context: Opening paragraph. The author announces a paid-content track for The Frontier Psychiatrists: textbook-style explainer chapters like this one, which he expects will not be opinion pieces.
statements.note: Own-newsletter content plan; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: I’m not gonna make you pay for it. Not yet anyway. It’s just gonna make you sign up for my subscription list. But eventually, behind that paywall, there’s content.
statements.context: Same opening paragraph, on the paywall in this and future explainer pieces. Readers who sign up are auto-comped for now; the author implies paid access will come later and paid content will sit behind the paywall.
statements.note: Own-newsletter monetization plan with an implied future paywall. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: We’re gonna start from neurons, and work our way up from there, that pretty soon, you’re gonna understand science and medicine just as well as I do.
statements.context: Series plan: the author intends a sequence of explainer chapters starting from neurons and working upward, and claims readers will soon understand science and medicine as well as he does.
statements.note: Own-newsletter content plan with rhetorical flourish; low forecast value.

statements.quote: I think, my own atheism notwithstanding, if Mr. Cuban successfully does something to reduce the cost of unbelievably expensive pharmaceuticals in America, it would be a legitimate heavenly miracle.
statements.context: Book 1 of a satirical sainthood hearing for Mark Cuban versus Martin Shkreli. Conditional on Mark Cuban's Cost Plus Drug Company (MCCPDC) actually reducing US drug costs; the 'miracle' framing signals the author's doubt that it will.
statements.confidence_phrase: if ... it would be a legitimate heavenly miracle
entities: Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drug Company (MCCPDC)
statements.note: Conditional inside satirical framing; the implied call is skepticism that Cuban will lower drug costs. Borderline.

statements.quote: And lo, he was prideful and vainglorious about his upcoming album which, I kid you not, is going to be called “God’s Gift”
statements.context: Pride entry in the seven-deadly-sins list about Martin Shkreli. Restates Shkreli's announced plan to release an album titled 'God's Gift'.
statements.note: Trivia about a third party's announced plan, adopted by the author; low forecast value.

statements.quote: The that workaround allows insane markups hidden from the rest of us and buried in our insurance premiums to go on even longer.
statements.context: Book 7 conclusion. The author argues Mark Cuban's cash-pay pharmacy (MCCPDC) is a workaround that lets hidden PBM and insurer markups buried in premiums persist longer instead of fixing the system.
entities: Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drug Company (MCCPDC)
statements.note: Systemic-effect claim. Text typo ('The that') quoted verbatim.

statements.quote: Depression , as a thing that haunts the minds and lives of millions of people, could be over 2 in five days. It doesn’t mean over forever. It does mean for now.
statements.context: Opening claim after FDA clearance of SAINT (Magnus, fMRI-guided accelerated TMS). The author asserts depression can be in remission within five days of treatment, citing the AJP randomized trial (79% remission active vs 13% sham).
statements.note: Efficacy claim drawn from a published RCT; borderline forward-looking (real-world generalization). Footnote marker '2' is part of the verbatim text.

statements.quote: It has to be made generally available through an extensive effort in manufacturing, distribution, systems of care, integration with existing systems, education of providers, sub-specialist training, new payment models, new staffing models, maybe even new business models
statements.context: The author says SAINT is FDA cleared but not yet obtainable; general availability will require manufacturing, distribution, care systems, provider and sub-specialist training, new payment and staffing models, and maybe new business models.
statements.note: Rollout-preconditions claim; compound list.

statements.quote: Everyone needs to get this treatment who needs to get this treatment when it is available. That is not now. That is soon. We need to be prepared. It is a moral imperative.
statements.context: Call to action: SAINT will be available soon (not now); the author says the field must prepare so everyone who needs the treatment gets it.
statements.note: Mixed normative ('needs to', 'moral imperative') and predictive ('That is not now. That is soon.').

statements.quote: What do you wanna bet your insurance isn’t gonna pay for it?
statements.context: Rhetorical question right after the call to action; the author predicts health insurers will not cover SAINT when it becomes available.
statements.note: Question in form, prediction in substance (insurers will not pay). Logged under the recall-first rule.

statements.quote: How long does this last? Well, we don’t know, but it’s something like 12 to 18 months on average.
statements.context: Footnote 2, defining 'over' as remission. The author estimates remission after SAINT lasts about 12 to 18 months on average, while admitting the duration is not known.
statements.confidence_phrase: we don’t know, but it’s something like
statements.note: Durability estimate; borderline forward-looking (expected duration of remission).

statements.quote: Medical malpractice insurance will not underwrite risk they cannot manage.
statements.context: TL;DR bullet 2 of the Texas gender-affirming-care essay. After Governor Abbott's directive defining gender-affirming care as child abuse, the author predicts malpractice carriers will refuse to underwrite physicians facing that unmanageable risk.
statements.note: TL;DR bullet; the body cites carrier calls (American Professional Agency, Allied World) that would not confirm continued coverage.

statements.quote: No malpractice insurance, no medical practice.* (it’s legal in Texas to practice without medical malpractice insurance, I just don’t know how many doctors are gonna want to do that!)
statements.context: TL;DR bullet 4. If carriers withdraw coverage, the author expects doctors to stop practicing, since few will practice uninsured in Texas.
statements.confidence_phrase: I just don’t know how many doctors are gonna want to do that
statements.note: Implied prediction that physicians will stop practicing or leave rather than go uninsured.

statements.quote: This, in turn, makes every employer-sponsored plan ERISA noncompliant , creating massive tax and fiduciary liability for employers and benefits brokers.
statements.context: TL;DR bullet 7. Chain of reasoning: banning gender-affirming care makes comprehensive care unavailable in Texas, so every employer-sponsored health plan becomes ERISA noncompliant, exposing employers and brokers to tax and fiduciary liability.
statements.note: Legal-consequence claim stated as fact; the liability is a predicted future exposure.

statements.quote: Therefore, bans on gender affirming care are subsequently effective bans on health insurance and it’s tax advantaged status.
statements.context: TL;DR bullet 8, the conclusion of the chain: state bans on gender-affirming care amount to bans on tax-advantaged employer health insurance.
statements.note: Restates bullet 7 as a conclusion; compound legal claim.

statements.quote: It’s a contravention of the standards of professional ethics for doctors, so should not be a needle in a haystack to find those with legal standing.
statements.context: The author asks the ACLU to arrange a malpractice suit against a physician who complied with the Texas reporting mandate, and predicts plaintiffs with legal standing will be easy to find.
statements.note: Advocacy plus prediction; 'should' here is probabilistic, not normative.

statements.quote: Of course it doesn’t end here, because refusing to see a patient because of the liability concern is, itself, something for which one could be found liable!
statements.context: After reporting that malpractice carriers gave no assurance of coverage, the author says physicians who decline patients over liability fears could themselves be held liable.
statements.note: Legal-exposure claim; borderline forward-looking.

statements.quote: It had a Gender Affirming Medicine program. Which has of course been put on pause. Which is a defensive legal move. It also opens the clinic up to almost unfathomable medico-legal liability.
statements.context: Texas Children's Hospital (Baylor College of Medicine's pediatric teaching hospital) paused its gender-affirming program after the directive; the author says this exposes the clinic to enormous malpractice liability under Texas DFPS's own definition of harm.
statements.note: Liability-exposure claim; forward-looking in that suits are expected.

statements.quote: This mandate has even opened the wormhole of legal horror that is the imminent collapse of the very Texas Department of Family Protective Services that is supposed to be the headsman for Governor Abbott’s politically popular execution
statements.context: The author predicts the Texas Department of Family and Protective Services, tasked with investigating families under Abbott's directive, faces imminent collapse because failures to investigate are themselves reportable to the same agency.
statements.note: Hyperbolic register but sincere; names DFPS collapse as imminent.

statements.quote: Failure to investigate any allegations on the part of that agency itself is reportable…to the same agency…with the same dire consequences. This could lead to a möbius loop of iterative reports of failures to protect kids.
statements.context: Continuation of the DFPS point: the agency's failure to investigate is itself reportable to DFPS; the author expects a self-referential loop of reports of failures to protect children.
statements.note: Hedged mechanism claim.

statements.quote: Political Action as new agency mission— over the objections of civil servants— is a poor employee retention plan in Child Protection circles, I would imagine.
statements.context: The author expects DFPS staff attrition as the agency is redirected to politically driven investigations; he cites Statesman reporting (Chuck Lindell) on employee objections.
statements.note: Hedged retention/attrition prediction.

statements.quote: If sued, she can and should loose. Subsequently her insurance would have to pay out on the claim. Medical Malpractice risk management starts to get nervous right about now.
statements.context: Hypothetical ER child psychiatrist bound by the Texas mandate: the author predicts she would lose a malpractice suit, her carrier would pay out, and carriers' risk management would react.
statements.confidence_phrase: can and should ... would have to
statements.note: Conditional on a hypothetical case; compound (loses suit, insurer pays, carriers get nervous).

statements.quote: Federal oversight of adequacy returns in 2023.
statements.context: In the ERISA/ACA section on network adequacy standards (time/distance, provider minimums, wait times), the author states federal oversight of network adequacy returns in 2023.
statements.note: Dated regulatory call; the federal agency is not named.

statements.quote: They make the standard of care illegal, and pretty quickly, the sequela of that — medical malpractice lawsuits, doctors fleeing your state, etc— create what some of us in healthcare advocacy would consider an opportunity
statements.context: Summing up: Abbott-style actions make the standard of care illegal, and the author predicts malpractice suits and physician flight from Texas will follow quickly, creating an ERISA-enforcement opportunity for advocates. Earlier he asks readers to imagine wait times 'when doctors start fleeing your state'.
statements.note: Compound: lawsuits, doctor flight, advocacy opportunity.

statements.quote: They create ERISA plan insufficiencies that are clear and unambiguous. This opens the door for definitive enforcement of the fiduciary rule under the CA 2020 law.
statements.context: The author expects the Texas ban to produce clear ERISA network insufficiencies, enabling definitive enforcement of the broker/plan-sponsor fiduciary rule from the Consolidated Appropriations Act (which he labels 'CA 2020'). He then argues a claim against a Texas employer would be 'unbelievably easy'.
statements.note: Enforcement-opportunity claim.

statements.quote: What is the number of providers available to provide gender affirming care to trans youth in the state of Texas? Answer : zero. All of them will go to jail if they do so.
statements.context: Worked example of an ERISA adequacy violation: the author asserts zero providers of gender-affirming care remain in Texas and that any who provide it will go to jail. Nearby he adds that families who seek care out of state 'still might' be prosecuted on return.
statements.note: Hyperbolic conditional ('will go to jail if they do so').

statements.quote: removing a medical subspecialty, and it’s associated care providers from the care available in a giant state like Texas causes every Texas employer – plan sponsors, most — and every Texas insurance plan selling ERISA compliant insurance A Serious Problem.
statements.context: Conclusion of the ERISA section: removing gender-affirming care and its providers from Texas creates a serious ERISA compliance problem for every Texas employer plan sponsor and every ERISA-compliant insurance plan sold in the state.
statements.note: Restates TL;DR bullets 7 and 8.

statements.quote: I’ve been waiting for the ability to have a ERISA attorney file lawsuits that are just going to totally crush noncompliant plans.
statements.context: 'Texas: I Left My Heart In You' section. The author expects ERISA lawsuits filed by an ERISA attorney to crush noncompliant health plans, now made easy by the Texas ban; this is also his own advocacy aim.
statements.confidence_phrase: are just going to totally crush
statements.note: Author's own litigation intent plus outcome prediction; coder may treat as CONTROL-adjacent.
